Doubting Thomas

An Evergreen Catholic Gospel Reflection · John 20:24–29
Journey Through the Reflection

What happens here?

Thomas is absent when the risen Jesus first appears to the disciples. When they tell him, “We have seen the Lord,” Thomas refuses to accept their testimony without seeing the wounds for himself.

Eight days later, Jesus comes again, despite the locked doors, and speaks directly to Thomas. He offers Thomas exactly the evidence he had demanded: “Put your finger here… and do not be unbelieving, but believe.”

Thomas responds with one of the clearest confessions of faith in the Gospel: “My Lord and my God!” Jesus then blesses all who will believe without having seen him with their own eyes.

The journey begins here

This reflection follows Thomas from honest resistance to a profound confession of faith. View the six-scene cinematic story, read the Gospel, consider its Catholic meaning, listen to a voice from the Tradition, and end with reflection and prayer.

Biblical Reflection

Thomas begins with a demand: he must see for himself. Jesus answers not with ridicule, but with presence, peace, and a personal invitation.

Follow Thomas from the disciples’ testimony and his resistance to his encounter with the risen Jesus, his confession, and the blessing for those who believe without seeing.

The lesson behind the image

Honest doubt can become deeper faith when it is brought to Christ.

The Sacred Passage

John 20:24–29

The risen Christ meets Thomas in his doubt and leads him to a direct confession of Jesus as Lord and God.

John 20:24–29

Now Thomas, one of the twelve, who is called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came.

The other disciples therefore said to him: “We have seen the Lord.” But he said to them: “Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”

Eight days later, his disciples were again inside, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came, although the doors were shut, and stood in their midst and said: “Peace be with you.”

Then he said to Thomas: “Put your finger here and see my hands. Bring your hand and put it into my side. Do not be unbelieving, but believe.”

Thomas answered him: “My Lord and my God!”

Jesus said to him: “Because you have seen me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and yet believe.”

One detail to notice

John moves immediately from Jesus’ invitation to Thomas’s confession. The Gospel does not explicitly say whether Thomas actually touched the wounds. The decisive moment is his recognition of the risen Jesus: “My Lord and my God!”

← Back to the Story Continue to the Catholic Point →

The Catholic Point

Christ meets honest doubt with mercy

Thomas’s doubt is serious, but he does not abandon the community of disciples. Eight days later he is still with them—and it is there, among the gathered disciples, that the risen Christ meets him.

Jesus does not humiliate Thomas. He addresses his exact struggle and invites him to move from resistance to faith. Christ’s wounds are not erased by the Resurrection; they have become signs of his victorious love.

Honest doubt becomes fruitful when it is brought to Christ rather than used as a reason to walk away from him.

Thomas’s answer, “My Lord and my God,” is more than relief that Jesus is alive. It is a confession of Christ’s divine identity and a personal act of surrender.

← Back to the Passage Continue to Catholic Tradition →

A Voice from the Catholic Tradition

St. Gregory the Great · Pope Francis

St. Gregory the Great teaches that Thomas’s struggle ultimately served the faith of later believers. Thomas saw the risen humanity of Christ and confessed the divine identity that bodily eyes alone could not reveal: “My Lord and my God!”

His resistance was not the end of the story. Christ’s wounds brought him to a confession that strengthens the Church’s witness to the bodily Resurrection.

Pope Francis emphasizes the mercy shown in this encounter. Jesus does not reject Thomas for his uncertainty. He returns, addresses Thomas personally, and offers him peace and the evidence he had requested.

In the wounds of Christ, Thomas discovers that he is loved, awaited, and understood. Doubt becomes a doorway to faith because it is met by the patience and tenderness of the risen Lord.

The golden nugget: Thomas saw the wounds of the risen man and confessed the God whom bodily eyes cannot see: “My Lord and my God.”

For Reflection

Doubt · Encounter · Faith
  1. What doubt, fear, or unanswered question do I need to bring honestly to Christ?
  2. Am I remaining close to the Church and the Christian community while I seek understanding?
  3. What would it mean for me to say to Jesus today, with greater sincerity, “My Lord and my God”?

Closing Prayer

Risen Lord Jesus, meet me in the places where my faith is weak or uncertain.

Keep me close to your Church, open my heart to your word, and help me recognize your wounded and victorious love.

Lead me beyond hesitation into the faith of Saint Thomas, so that I may confess you sincerely as my Lord and my God.

Amen.
